rationale: The remaining gap asks what the durable term regression does at cluster level, and this turn answers it conditionally from the two message paths that decide it rather than spending an execution on a sequence whose outcome those paths already fix. A node that has gone backwards sends a lower term than its peers hold: a vote request with a term below the receiver's current term returns immediately on the receiver without a vote, and an appendEntries carrying an older term is likewise ignored, so while peers are at the higher term the regressed node cannot win an election or make progress; the first message it does receive from a peer at the higher term is an appendEntries whose term exceeds its own, and that path adopts the higher term and makes it a follower, which is the repair. The conditional is therefore whether a higher-term peer is reachable: if one is, the regression is transient and the cluster is consistent again as soon as the two talk; if the node is alone - which is exactly what the single-node witness exercised, where it led at the lower term - its own decisions are made on a term basis the rest of the cluster has already superseded, and because setCurrentTerm persisted the lower value the same starting point survives a restart while it remains isolated. One harm is excluded by source and I say so: votes are recorded per term and the duplicate check refuses a different candidate in a term the node has already voted in, so revisiting an earlier term does not hand out a second vote; what the regression removes is the node's memory that it had observed a higher term, which is the property that keeps a stale candidate from campaigning as if nothing had happened. I record this as a conditional interpretation with its sources, answer the gap with the condition stated, and do not assert a new defect beyond the regression already witnessed.

Peers ignore a node whose term is behind: appendEntries returns immediately when the request term is below the receiver's current term, and a vote request with an older term returns before anything else is considered, so a node sitting at the regressed term cannot make progress with peers that are at the term it had adopted - not by replicating and not by winning an election. The repair is the same path read the other way: an appendEntries whose term is above the receiver's current term makes it a follower and stores the higher term, so the first heartbeat from a peer at that higher term restores the node's term and the cluster is consistent again. The consequence is therefore conditional on reachability rather than uniformly harmful: with a higher-term peer reachable the durable inconsistency is transient and self-correcting within one heartbeat interval, and with the node isolated - the state the single-node witness already exercised, where it went on to lead at the lower term - its decisions are taken on a term basis the rest of the cluster has abandoned, and because setCurrentTerm persisted that value, a restart while still isolated resumes from it. What the regression does remove is the node's knowledge that it had seen a higher term at all, which is the observation Raft leans on to keep stale candidates from campaigning as though nothing had happened. I answer the gap with that condition and keep the claim at the regression already witnessed rather than inflating it into a safety violation.
